newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.A. BREWERIES TARGETS AFRICA, E.EUROPE, CHINA.
newsitem.headline: S.A. BREWERIES TARGETS AFRICA, E.EUROPE, CHINA.

text.p: Brewing giant South African Breweries is making sure the country's re-entry into world markets is based not just on gold and mining, but on beer.

After supplying nearly every drinker at home, the maker of Castle and Lion has a plan for global success that seems simple: target ordinary people in the developing world, the most numerous beer drinkers on earth.

The company that calls itself Africa's largest industrial group has spread across the continent, through eastern Europe and into China as it stakes out a place as a key brewer to the world's emerging markets.
Expansion has been swift, especially since the collapse of apartheid made business easier to do.
SAB has moved into a new country every few months on average, with Poland and Romania the latest to fall.
COMPANY PLANS FURTHER OVERSEAS EXPANSION
Company strategists have decided they can go much further.

In September SAB announced it was considering tapping the market to the tune of as much as two billion rand ($450 million) to finance further overseas expansion in the 15 countries where it is already present.
"Part of the fund is earmarked to pay for additional investment in Romania and Poland, one new brewery in each," Group Secretary Andrew Tonkinson told Reuters.
"We will also expand in China's Liaoning province."
Analysts toasted the plan to boost activities in what is SAB's only significant avenue for growth since its share of the home market stands at an astounding 97 percent.
The company says its near-monopoly at home is due to smart business, not government help or suspect practices.
SAB, now 101 years old, has dominated the market since merging with its two biggest rivals in the 1950s.

It fought off local and foreign attempts to muscle in on its terrain in the 1960s and 70s, after which political instability deterred most from trying. Interest in competing has now revived but has made no real difference to SAB's dominance.
International Beer Interests is its fastest growing division, already accounting for a quarter of trading profit and hoping to earn two thirds as much as the home division by the end of the century.
A third of the 3.5 billion litres of beer SAB brews each year is produced outside South Africa. It is the world's fifth biggest brewer.
Pretax profit for the year to the end of March 1996 was three billion rand, 18 percent up on the year before, on turnover of 32.6 billion rand.
The company that says Africa is its natural marketplace made some of its first foreign forays into neighbouring states.
It now has controlling stakes in the state breweries of Tanzania, Zambia and, since last year, Mozambique.
In 1993 it bought 79 percent of Kobanyai Sorgyar, Hungary's biggest brewer, establishing what it says is a beachhead for expansion into an opening eastern Europe.

Last year SAB spread into nearby Poland, one of Europe's fastest-growing beer markets where it took 28 percent of Lech Browary Wielkopolski, and east into Romania where it took control of SC Vulturul SA.
On Monday, Kompania Piwna SA, a company formed by SAB and Poland's Euro Agro Centrum SA, bought a 52 percent stake in the Polish Tychy brewery for $75 million.
In northeast China it has bought into Shenyang Brewery to get a foothold in a billion-throat market that few major brewers dare ignore.
NO PLANS TO ENTER SATURATED WESTERN MARKETS
Sticking to their philosophy, SAB chiefs have no plans to enter highly competitive and saturated Western markets.
"Our focus is in other developing markets with potential for rapid growth from a low base or, if not rapid, then substantial growth over time," said Tonkinson.
"The market characteristics have a thread running through."

Unlike rivals such as U.S. Anheuser-Busch, the world's biggest brewer which promotes its flagship Budweiser globally, the South Africans prefer to build up existing local brands for average consumers rather than the young and affluent.
Lion, with its slogan "brewed in Africa", will stay in Africa while northeastern China will still drink their Snowflake, largely unaware of South African involvement.
With a market capitalisation of 40.86 billion rand, SAB is South Africa's third-biggest conglomerate behind the Oppenheimer family's Anglo American Corp and De Beers.
Its ambitious expansion plans are unprecedented for a company in a country cut off for so long from the outside.
The brewers will face fierce competition abroad that they have not had to deal with at home, but say they have their own strong points and are not overly worried.

"Our trick is that we have long experience brewing high quality beer in circumstances that are rudimentary, with minimal infrastructure -- or none, in which case we put it in ourselves as in Tanzania," said Tonkinson
DOING BEST IN AFRICAN MARKETS
He said the company was doing best in African markets where their main competitors when they entered were dearer imported bottled beers.

"We are the main players in our own backyard, sub-Saharan Africa," he said. "In eastern Europe we face several difficulties. It is closer to European and U.S. competition so it is attractive to other brewers."
Despite its rapid growth abroad and diversification into South African shops and hotels, SAB says it expects to stay focused on brewing beer for its home market.
Consumption is edging up by 3-4 percent a year as black drinkers continue a slow shift to clear lager beer and away from sorghum beer, a traditional murky unpasteurised brew.
With per capita consumption at 56 litres a year -- compared to 85 litres for Americans, 100 for Britons and 138 for Germans -- there is still some growth to hope for. ($=4.5 rand)
